idiom_name: one CGI program (or one libmicrohttpd URL handler) per page
implementation_notes: CGI is the pattern in its most literal form: the server selects a program per URL, and the program reads the request from meta-variables (REQUEST_METHOD, QUERY_STRING, PATH_INFO) and writes headers plus body on stdout (RFC 3875), so the page controller is the program's main(). The long-running alternative embeds GNU libmicrohttpd and dispatches inside a single MHD_AccessHandlerCallback that receives (url, method, ...) - the page controller becomes a branch or a handler-table lookup, and MHD_create_response_from_buffer plus MHD_queue_response replace redirects and rendered views. Nothing supplies routing, request parsing or view rendering, so the controller skeleton and any behaviour shared between pages (a common check_request helper called from each page) are hand-written; the per-page program is still justified for simple deployments where each page has its own lifetime.
pitfalls: CGI meta-variables are fully attacker-controlled: parse lengths explicitly, never pass them to system()/popen(), and always emit Content-Length or close the response cleanly.
Process-per-request startup dominates latency under load and makes per-page state impossible to share; consolidate into one daemon (libmicrohttpd threading mode) when traffic grows.
Shared code is linked into every page program, so an API change must be recompiled across all of them or the pages drift onto different versions of the helper.
